options: reinvested in new credit card receivables.
used to retire the senior tranche first.
passed through to investors each month.
questions.explanation: In the lockout (revolving) period principal is reinvested to buy new receivables; investors receive only interest. Principal is passed through only in the amortisation period or after an early amortisation trigger.

questions.stem: An early (rapid) amortisation provision in a credit card ABS is designed to:
options: allow the issuer to call the securities at par.
protect investors by starting principal repayment if collateral performance deteriorates.
extend the life of the deal when rates rise.
questions.explanation: Triggers such as low excess spread end the revolving period early so investors are repaid before the collateral weakens further. It shortens, not extends, the deal and is not an issuer call.

questions.stem: A CLO holds 400m of leveraged loans yielding 8%. Its debt tranches total 360m with a weighted cost of 6%, annual fees are 2m and the equity tranche is 40m. Assuming no defaults, the annual return to the equity tranche is *closest* to:
questions.explanation: Collateral income 32m − debt cost 21.6m − fees 2m = 8.4m; 8.4 ÷ 40 = 21%. 26% ignores fees (10.4 ÷ 40). 2% is simply the 8% − 6% spread with no leverage.

questions.stem: An ABS deal has collateral of 420m backing bonds of 400m: senior 300m, mezzanine 60m and subordinated 40m. If collateral losses are 70m, the mezzanine tranche loses:
options: 0m
questions.explanation: Overcollateralisation absorbs the first 20m (420 − 400). The subordinated tranche absorbs the next 40m. The remaining 70 − 20 − 40 = 10m hits the mezzanine. 30m ignores the overcollateralisation; 0m ignores the subordinated tranche's limit.

questions.stem: An investor worried about the credit quality of a monoline insurer that guarantees an ABS tranche is concerned about which feature?
options: Excess spread
External credit enhancement
Subordination
questions.explanation: A financial guarantee is external enhancement; the tranche's protection depends on the guarantor's creditworthiness. Subordination and excess spread are internal and do not depend on a third party.

questions.stem: Compared with auto loan ABS, credit card ABS are *most* distinct because the underlying receivables are:
options: secured by the vehicles financed.
always issued to subprime borrowers.
non-amortising, with no scheduled principal payments.
questions.explanation: Credit card balances revolve and have no scheduled principal, hence the lockout and amortisation periods. Auto loans amortise and are secured by vehicles; credit card ABS are not limited to subprime borrowers.

questions.stem: In a CLO, the collateral manager's role is to:
options: actively buy and sell loans in the portfolio within the deal's rules.
collect payments from mortgage borrowers.
guarantee the senior tranche against defaults.
questions.explanation: CLOs are actively managed: the collateral manager trades leveraged loans subject to quality and coverage tests. It does not guarantee tranches; mortgage collection is a servicer role in MBS.

flashcards.back: Bank issuer, assets stay on balance sheet; dual recourse (bank + cover pool); dynamic cover pool.
Subordination, overcollateralisation, excess spread, reserve accounts.
Financial guarantees and letters of credit; exposes investors to the provider's credit risk.

flashcards.front: Loss allocation in a senior/subordinated structure
flashcards.back: Bottom-up: most junior tranche absorbs losses first.
Collateral yield − tranche coupons − fees.
Principal repayments are reinvested in new receivables; investors receive only interest.
Ends the revolving period and starts principal repayment if collateral performance deteriorates.
CDO backed by leveraged loans; actively managed by a collateral manager; equity tranche earns the residual.

modules.title: Mortgage-Backed Security (MBS) Instrument and Market Features
modules.summary: Covers residential mortgage features, agency vs non-agency RMBS, pass-through securities and prepayment measures (SMM, CPR, PSA), contraction and extension risk, CMOs (sequential-pay, PAC/support) that redistribute prepayment risk, and CMBS with their call protection and balloon risk.

acca.note: ACCA does not cover mortgage-backed securities, prepayment conventions or CMO structures. Treat this LM as new.

lessons.title: Residential mortgages and RMBS types

cards.title: Mortgage design choices
rows: Commonly 15–30 years (US); longer in some countries
Fixed, adjustable (ARM), hybrid (fixed then floating), convertible
Allowed freely or subject to prepayment penalties
Recourse (can pursue borrower) or non-recourse (only the property)

cards.title: Loan-to-value ratio
where: higher LTV = less borrower equity = higher default and loss risk
cards.note: Example: 400,000 loan on a 500,000 home → LTV 80%.

cards.title: Non-recourse and strategic default
cards.body:
With a **non-recourse** loan, the lender can only take the house. If the house is worth much less than the loan (negative equity), a borrower who *can* pay may choose to walk away: a **strategic default**.

Recourse loans reduce this incentive because the lender can pursue the borrower's other assets.

cards.title: Agency vs non-agency RMBS
rows: Ginnie Mae (US govt full faith and credit); Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac (GSEs)
Conforming: meet size, LTV and credit standards
Real: needs credit enhancement and ratings

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: For agency MBS the main risk is **prepayment risk**, not credit risk. For non-agency MBS, investors face both, which is why subordination and other credit enhancement (from LM 18) appear in non-agency deals.

lessons.title: Pass-throughs, prepayment and WAL

cards.title: Mortgage pass-through securities
cards.body:
A **pass-through** passes the pool's monthly cash flows (interest, scheduled principal and prepayments) to investors pro rata, minus fees.

**Pass-through rate** = pool mortgage rate − servicing fee − guarantee fee. E.g., 6.5% − 0.25% − 0.25% = **6.0%**.

Because borrowers can prepay, the timing of principal is uncertain: that is **prepayment risk**.

cards.title: Prepayment risk: two sides
rows: Principal returned early, reinvested at lower rates; price upside capped (negative convexity)
Life lengthens just when the investor wants money back to invest at higher rates

cards.title: Prepayment measures
where: single monthly mortality: % of balance prepaid in a month
cards.note: Do not just multiply SMM by 12.

cards.title: PSA benchmark
cards.body:
**100 PSA**: CPR starts at 0.2% in month 1, rises 0.2% a month to 6% at month 30, then stays at 6%.

**150 PSA** = 1.5 × that path.
- Month 10: 1.5 × 2% = **3% CPR**.
- Month 40: 1.5 × 6% = **9% CPR** → SMM = 1 − 0.91^{1/12} = **0.783%**.

SMM 0.5% → CPR = 1 − 0.995^{12} = **5.84%**.

cards.title: Weighted average life (WAL)
cards.note: Example: principal 30, 50, 20 in years 1, 2, 3 → WAL = (30 + 100 + 60) ÷ 100 = 1.9 years. Faster prepayments → shorter WAL.

lessons.title: CMOs and commercial MBS

cards.title: CMOs: redistributing prepayment risk
cards.body:
A **collateralised mortgage obligation (CMO)** carves pass-through cash flows into tranches with different exposure to prepayment risk. It *redistributes* risk; it does not eliminate it.

**Sequential-pay**: all principal (scheduled + prepayments) goes to tranche A until it is retired, then to B, etc. Early tranches bear more contraction risk; later tranches more extension risk but get protection from contraction.

cards.title: PAC and support tranches
cards.body:
A **planned amortisation class (PAC)** tranche receives principal on a fixed schedule as long as prepayments stay within a band (the PAC collar, e.g., 100–300 PSA).

The **support (companion)** tranche absorbs the variability: it takes extra principal when prepayments are fast and is paid later when they are slow.

PAC: more predictable, lower yield. Support: most prepayment risk, higher yield.

cards.title: Commercial MBS (CMBS)
cards.body:
Backed by loans on income-producing property (offices, malls, apartments). Lenders focus on the property's income:

**DSCR = NOI ÷ Debt service** (higher is safer)
**LTV = Loan ÷ Appraised value** (lower is safer)

CMBS loans are usually **non-recourse** and often **balloon** loans: a large principal is due at maturity. **Balloon risk** = the borrower cannot refinance, extending the loan (a form of extension risk).

cards.title: CMBS call protection
rows: Prepayment lockout; defeasance (borrower buys Treasuries replicating remaining payments); prepayment penalty points; yield maintenance (penalty makes lender whole)
Sequential tranching by rating: lower tranches absorb losses and prepayments are paid to senior tranches first

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: CMBS investors face much **less prepayment risk** than RMBS investors because of strong call protection, but more **credit and balloon risk**. Residential: prepayment-driven. Commercial: credit-driven.

questions.stem: A borrower takes a 400,000 mortgage to buy a home valued at 500,000. The loan-to-value ratio is:
questions.explanation: LTV = 400,000 ÷ 500,000 = 80%. 125% inverts the ratio. 20% is the borrower's equity share.

questions.stem: Compared with a recourse mortgage, a non-recourse mortgage is *most likely* to:
options: allow the lender to claim the borrower's other assets after foreclosure.
have a lower default rate, because borrowers have more equity.
increase the risk of strategic default when the property's value falls below the loan balance.
questions.explanation: With non-recourse loans the lender can only take the property, so a borrower in negative equity may walk away even though able to pay. Recourse loans allow claims on other assets.

questions.stem: For an investor in agency RMBS guaranteed by Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac, the *primary* risk is typically:
options: prepayment risk.
credit risk of the underlying borrowers.
currency risk.
questions.explanation: Agency guarantees largely remove borrower credit risk, leaving uncertainty about the timing of principal (prepayment risk) as the key risk. Non-agency RMBS carry significant credit risk; currency risk is not inherent.

questions.stem: Non-agency RMBS differ from agency RMBS mainly because they:
options: carry the full faith and credit of the US government.
require credit enhancement because there is no government or GSE guarantee.
are backed only by conforming loans.
questions.explanation: Private-label deals have no guarantee, so subordination and other enhancement are used. Agency deals use conforming loans; only Ginnie Mae carries the full faith and credit guarantee.

questions.stem: A mortgage pool has a single monthly mortality rate of 0.5%. The conditional prepayment rate is *closest* to:
questions.explanation: CPR = 1 − (1 − 0.005)^{12} = 5.84%. 6.00% simply multiplies SMM by 12, ignoring that each month's prepayments apply to a smaller balance. 0.50% is the monthly rate.

questions.stem: A pool is prepaying at 150 PSA. The CPR in month 40 and month 10, respectively, are:
options: 9% and 3%
9% and 2%
6% and 2%
questions.explanation: 100 PSA: CPR = 0.2% × month up to 6% at month 30. At 150 PSA: month 40 = 1.5 × 6% = 9%; month 10 = 1.5 × 2% = 3%. 6% and 2% are the 100 PSA values; 9% and 2% scales month 40 but not month 10.

questions.stem: A pass-through's pool has a beginning monthly balance of 200 million and scheduled principal of 0.4 million. If the SMM is 0.6%, the prepayment for the month is *closest* to:
options: 0.0024 million
1.1976 million
1.2000 million
questions.explanation: Prepayment = SMM × (beginning balance − scheduled principal) = 0.006 × 199.6m = 1.1976m. 1.2000m forgets to subtract scheduled principal. 0.0024m applies SMM to the scheduled principal only.

questions.stem: When mortgage rates fall sharply, holders of mortgage pass-through securities are *most* exposed to:
options: balloon risk.
extension risk.
contraction risk.
questions.explanation: Falling rates trigger refinancing and faster prepayments, shortening the security's life and forcing reinvestment at lower rates: contraction risk. Extension risk arises when rates rise; balloon risk is a CMBS concept.

questions.stem: An MBS is expected to repay principal of 30 in year 1, 50 in year 2 and 20 in year 3. Its weighted average life is:
options: 1.9 years
2.0 years
3.0 years
questions.explanation: WAL = (1 × 30 + 2 × 50 + 3 × 20) ÷ 100 = 190 ÷ 100 = 1.9 years. 2.0 is an unweighted average of the years. 3.0 is the final maturity.

questions.stem: In a sequential-pay CMO with tranches A, B and C, an increase in prepayment speed will *most likely*:
options: shorten tranche C's average life first.
shorten tranche A's average life first, while C's principal is still deferred.
be shared pro rata by all three tranches.
questions.explanation: All principal, including prepayments, goes to A until it is retired, then to B, then C. Faster prepayments shorten A's life first. Allocation is sequential, not pro rata.

questions.stem: In a CMO with a planned amortisation class (PAC) tranche and a support tranche, if prepayments are faster than expected but within the PAC collar:
options: both tranches receive principal pro rata.
the PAC tranche receives the excess principal.
the support tranche absorbs the excess principal, keeping the PAC on schedule.
questions.explanation: The support tranche exists to absorb prepayment variability so the PAC follows its schedule within the collar. That makes the support tranche shorter here (contraction) and the PAC stable.

questions.stem: A commercial property has net operating income of 1.2 million and annual debt service of 1.0 million. Its debt service coverage ratio is:
questions.explanation: DSCR = NOI ÷ debt service = 1.2 ÷ 1.0 = 1.20×. 0.83× inverts the ratio; 2.20× adds the two figures.

questions.stem: A CMBS borrower who wishes to prepay must purchase a portfolio of government securities that replicates the remaining loan payments. This call-protection feature is:
options: a prepayment lockout.
defeasance.
yield maintenance.
questions.explanation: Defeasance substitutes government securities for the loan's remaining payments. Yield maintenance is a cash penalty that makes the lender whole; a lockout simply prohibits prepayment for a period.

questions.stem: A mortgage pool is prepaying at 200 PSA. In month 20, the single monthly mortality rate is *closest* to:
questions.explanation: At 100 PSA, month-20 CPR = 0.2% × 20 = 4%; at 200 PSA, 8%. SMM = 1 − (1 − 0.08)^{1/12} = 0.69%. 0.67% simply divides 8% by 12. 8.00% is the annual CPR.

questions.stem: A pool's SMM is 0.8%. Its CPR is *closest* to:
questions.explanation: CPR = 1 − (1 − 0.008)^{12} = 9.19%. 9.60% multiplies by 12 (ignores the declining balance). 0.80% is the monthly rate.

questions.stem: A CMBS tranche has expected principal of 40 in year 1, 35 in year 2 and 25 in year 3. Its weighted average life is *closest* to:
options: 2.15 years
1.85 years
2.00 years
questions.explanation: WAL = (1 × 40 + 2 × 35 + 3 × 25) ÷ 100 = 185 ÷ 100 = 1.85 years. 2.00 is the unweighted average; 2.15 reverses the principal amounts (25, 35, 40).

questions.stem: Compared with RMBS investors, CMBS investors *most likely* face:
options: the same risks, because both are backed by mortgages.
more prepayment risk and less credit risk.
less prepayment risk but significant balloon risk.
questions.explanation: CMBS loans have strong call protection (lockouts, defeasance, yield maintenance), so prepayment risk is low, but they are typically non-recourse balloon loans, creating balloon (refinancing) and credit risk.

questions.stem: An investor wants mortgage exposure with the *most* predictable principal repayment schedule over a range of prepayment speeds. The *best* choice is:
options: the PAC tranche of a CMO.
the support tranche of a CMO.
a mortgage pass-through security.
questions.explanation: The PAC follows a fixed schedule as long as prepayments stay within the collar, because the support tranche absorbs variability. The support tranche is the least predictable; a pass-through passes all prepayment variability straight through.

questions.stem: If interest rates rise sharply, the holder of the *last* tranche in a sequential-pay CMO is *most* exposed to:
options: default risk from the GSE.
extension risk.
contraction risk.
questions.explanation: Rising rates slow prepayments, so the final tranche waits even longer for principal: extension risk. Contraction risk comes with falling rates; GSE default risk is not the issue here.
